Language: Python 3.12+, standard library only at runtime
Interface: command-line program run as `python -m parking_fee <path>` with the src directory on the import path
Structure: src/parking_fee/ containing tariff.py (tariff data only), parsing.py (file reading, JSON parsing and ticket validation), calculator.py (pure fee calculation, no I/O), cli.py (argument handling, output, exit codes) and __main__.py
Tariff: one frozen data structure keyed by vehicle type, with grace minutes, rate per started hour, cap per 1440-minute block and the lost-ticket penalty; values as in FR-007
Arithmetic: integers only. Compute minutes since a fixed epoch as date(y, m, d).toordinal() * 1440 + hour * 60 + minute, so duration is a plain integer difference. Never use timedelta.total_seconds() or any float. Use integer ceiling division, for example (r + 59) // 60. State this in the plan.
Timestamps: validate with an explicit pattern using [0-9] (never \d or str.isdigit, which accept non-ASCII digits), exactly 16 characters, then check month, day, hour and minute ranges via the date constructor and explicit hour and minute bounds
File reading: check the argument count with len(argv) only; do not use argparse or any option parser. Read bytes with open(path, "rb"). A path that is not a regular file, or any OSError, gives the read error.
JSON parsing: read bytes, reject empty input and any input starting with the UTF-8 byte-order mark bytes EF BB BF, decode strictly as UTF-8 (not utf-8-sig), then parse with json.loads using an object_pairs_hook that rejects duplicate keys and a parse_constant hook that rejects NaN, Infinity and -Infinity. Treat UnicodeDecodeError, JSONDecodeError, ValueError and RecursionError (deeply nested input) all as the JSON error, so no stack trace is ever shown.
Output: write bytes to sys.stdout.buffer and sys.stderr.buffer, ending each line with exactly "\n" and never "\r\n" (Windows would otherwise translate newlines). Serialize the result with json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":")). main(argv) returns the exit code, 0 or 2, and nothing else is printed.
Error handling: one function maps each failed validation to its exact FR-013 message in the specified order. No blanket except clause that hides unexpected bugs.
Files: do not create pyproject.toml, requirements files, CI configuration or any file outside src/ other than the plan artifacts under specs/.
Tests and harness: tests/ and .harness/ are owned by the human engineer. Do not plan or generate tasks that create or modify them. Provide a table mapping every AC (AC-001 through AC-042) to the module that satisfies it and the test file that will verify it, as traceability only.

 # Parking Fee Calculator Constitution
 
 ## Core Principles
 
 ### I. Modular Separation of Concerns
 The application MUST separate input parsing and validation, tariff definition, fee
 calculation, and command-line handling. The fee calculation MUST be a pure function
 with no input/output operations. The command-line layer MUST remain thin.
 
 ### II. Data-Driven Tariff
 The grace period, hourly rates, daily cap, and any penalties MUST be defined as data
 in one tariff module, separate from the fee calculation function. This keeps tariff
 policy distinct from calculation logic.
 
 ### III. Integer Money and Durations
 Money MUST be represented as whole rupees using integers. Durations MUST be
 represented as whole seconds or minutes using integers. Floats MUST NOT be used for
 money or durations, including during parsing.
 
 ### IV. Deterministic Behavior
 The same input file MUST produce byte-identical output. The program MUST NOT use
 randomness, read the system clock, or make network calls. The feature specification
 MUST state every ordering and rounding rule, including output serialization rules;
 the implementation MUST follow those rules.
 
 ### V. Explicit Input and CLI Contract
 The command line MUST accept exactly one input file path argument and emit a JSON
 result on stdout on success, with exit code 0. Invalid input MUST produce exit code 2
 and a single-line error message on stderr. Expected errors MUST NOT produce stack
 traces. Input validation and error handling MUST be explicit, and invalid input MUST
 never produce partial results.
 
 ## Runtime and Security Constraints
 
 The tool MUST use Python 3.12 or later and only the Python standard library at
 runtime. Development tools including pytest, pytest-cov, ruff, and bandit are
 permitted. The program MUST read only the input file supplied to it.
 
 Secrets MUST NOT be exposed in source code. Credentials, API keys, and `.env` files
 MUST NOT be committed. The program MUST NOT use `eval`, `exec`, `pickle`, or shell
 execution.
 
 ## Quality and Implementation Boundaries
 
 An independent harness MUST enforce all of these quality gates: ruff reports zero
 errors; bandit reports zero medium- or high-severity findings; all tests pass; line
 coverage of `src/` is at least 90%; and every acceptance criterion in the
 specification maps to at least one automated test.
 
 The human engineer owns `tests/` and `.harness/`. Generated task lists MUST NOT
 include tasks to create or modify those directories, though tasks MAY reference
 them for traceability. During implementation and repair, application code MUST be
 implemented in `src/` only. The coding agent MUST NOT modify the specification,
 `tests/`, or `.harness/`; delete or weaken tests or assertions; lower thresholds;
 disable lint or security checks; bypass mandatory harness gates; or manually edit
 recorded harness results. Specification artifacts MAY be changed only through the
 Spec Kit commands `specify`, `clarify`, `plan`, and `tasks`; every legitimate
 specification change MUST record its reason. Marking completed tasks in `tasks.md` 
 during implementation is permitted.
 
 Solutions MUST prefer simplicity and maintainability over unnecessary complexity.
 
 ## Governance
 
 This constitution governs the Parking Fee Calculator and its implementation
 workflow. Amendments MUST be made through the Spec Kit constitution workflow, state
 their reason, and update the version and last-amended date. Version numbers follow
 semantic versioning: MAJOR for backward-incompatible governance changes, MINOR for
 new or materially expanded principles or sections, and PATCH for clarifications and
 non-semantic refinements.
 
 Implementation and repair work MUST be reviewed against this constitution. The
 independent harness MUST verify the stated quality gates; any failure blocks
 acceptance until resolved without weakening or bypassing the gates.

 # Feature Specification: Parking Fee Calculator
 
 **Feature Branch**: `not created by this command`
 
 **Created**: 2026-10-31
 
 **Status**: Draft
 
 **Input**: User description: "Build a Parking Fee Calculator that reads one parking ticket from a JSON file and prints the fee."
 
 ## Clarifications
 
 ### Session 2026-10-31
 
 - Q: How should a sole command-line argument that starts with "-" (for example --help) be treated: as a file path, or as an option? → A: As a file path.
 - Q: Must every digit in a timestamp be an ASCII digit 0 through 9, with other Unicode digits rejected? → A: Yes; timestamp digits must be ASCII 0-9 only.
 - Q: What should count as an unreadable input file, including when the supplied path refers to a directory? → A: A path that is not a regular file, or whose contents cannot be fully opened and read as bytes.
 - Q: How should a UTF-8 byte-order mark at the very start of the input file be treated? → A: Reject it with the specified JSON error.
 
 ## User Scenarios & Testing *(mandatory)*
 
 ### User Story 1 - Calculate a parking fee (Priority: P1)
 
 A parking attendant supplies one ticket file and receives the duration, parking fee, any lost-ticket penalty, total fee, and vehicle type in a predictable result.
 
 **Why this priority**: Producing the correct bill for a valid ticket is the feature's primary value.
 
 **Independent Test**: Supply one valid ticket and verify its exit status and exact output line. The example ticket is covered by AC-015.
 
 **Acceptance Scenarios**:
 
 1. **Given** a valid car ticket for 190 minutes, **When** its file path is supplied, **Then** the exact result in AC-015 is printed.
 2. **Given** a valid two-wheeler ticket, **When** its file path is supplied, **Then** the fee uses the two-wheeler tariff, as verified by AC-016.
 
 ### User Story 2 - Apply grace, tariff, caps, and penalties (Priority: P1)
 
 A parking attendant receives a bill that accounts for the grace period, hourly rounding, full 24-hour blocks, daily caps, and a lost ticket.
 
 **Why this priority**: Correct and consistent application of the published tariff prevents incorrect charges.
 
 **Independent Test**: Supply valid tickets at each specified duration boundary and with or without a lost ticket; compare each complete result line with AC-001 through AC-023.
 
 **Acceptance Scenarios**:
 
 1. **Given** a stay of 15 minutes or less, **When** it is billed, **Then** its parking fee is zero (AC-001 through AC-004).
 2. **Given** a stay longer than 15 minutes, **When** it is billed, **Then** each started hour and each 24-hour block is charged according to the tariff (AC-005 through AC-019).
 3. **Given** a lost ticket, **When** it is billed, **Then** the penalty is added even if the parking fee is zero (AC-020 and AC-021).
 
 ### User Story 3 - Receive a precise error for invalid input (Priority: P1)
 
 A user receives one stable, actionable error message when the argument, file, or ticket is invalid, without a partial result.
 
 **Why this priority**: Clear failure behavior lets users correct an input instead of mistaking an invalid ticket for a valid bill.
 
 **Independent Test**: Supply each invalid argument/file/ticket vector and verify the exit status, empty standard output, exact error line, and precedence in AC-024 through AC-033 and AC-040 through AC-042.
 
 **Acceptance Scenarios**:
 
 1. **Given** an invalid argument count, **When** the command is invoked, **Then** the argument-count error wins over file errors (AC-024 and AC-033).
 2. **Given** a ticket with multiple invalid fields, **When** it is read, **Then** the first failing validation in the specified order determines the sole error (AC-033).
 
 ### Edge Cases
 
 - Valid zero-duration, grace-period, hourly-rounding, and single- and multi-day tariff cases cover both vehicle types, including lost-ticket handling (AC-001 through AC-023).
 - Additional valid cases cover hourly-cap boundaries, a year transition, and a leap-year transition (AC-034 through AC-039).
 - Invalid argument counts produce the argument-count error (AC-024); missing input paths and directory paths produce the file-read error (AC-025); a sole `--help` argument is treated as a missing input-file path (AC-040).
 - Empty, wrongly encoded, malformed, duplicate-key, or byte-order-mark-prefixed JSON produces the JSON error; valid JSON with a non-object top-level value produces the object error (AC-026, AC-027, and AC-042).
 - Invalid entry and exit timestamps, including an entry timestamp with fullwidth digits, produce their respective timestamp errors (AC-028, AC-029, and AC-041).
 - Invalid vehicle types, invalid lost-ticket values, earlier exit times, and validation-precedence conflicts produce the defined errors (AC-030 through AC-033).
 
 ## Requirements *(mandatory)*
 
 ### Functional Requirements
 
 - **FR-001**: The command MUST accept exactly one command-line argument, interpreted as the input file path, even when it starts with `-` (for example, `--help`).
 - **FR-002**: The command MUST report a missing path, a path that does not refer to a regular file (including a directory), or a file whose contents cannot be fully opened and read as bytes using the specified file-read error.
 - **FR-003**: The input file MUST contain valid UTF-8 JSON whose top-level value is an object. An empty file, invalid UTF-8, a UTF-8 byte-order mark at the start, invalid JSON, or an object with duplicate property names MUST use the specified JSON error. Properties other than `entry`, `exit`, `vehicle_type`, and `lost_ticket` MUST be ignored.
 - **FR-004**: The object MUST contain string values for `entry`, `exit`, and `vehicle_type`. `lost_ticket` MAY be omitted; when present it MUST be a JSON boolean, and omission MUST mean false.
 - **FR-005**: Each timestamp MUST be exactly 16 characters in the form `YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM`, with zero-padded fields using ASCII digits `0` through `9` only, no seconds or time zone, and a real calendar date and time.
 - **FR-006**: The exit timestamp MUST be equal to or later than the entry timestamp. Duration MUST be the whole number of minutes between the two timestamps; equal timestamps yield zero.
 - **FR-007**: The default tariff data used by the calculation MUST use the following values:
 
   | Tariff item | two_wheeler | car |
   |---|---:|---:|
   | Rate per started hour | 20 rupees | 40 rupees |
   | Cap per 24-hour block | 150 rupees | 300 rupees |
 
   The grace period is 15 minutes for either vehicle type. The lost-ticket penalty is 200 rupees for either vehicle type.
 - **FR-008**: For a duration of 15 minutes or less, the parking fee MUST be zero. The lost-ticket penalty, if any, MUST still apply.
 - **FR-009**: For a duration longer than 15 minutes, the full stay duration MUST be billed; the grace period MUST NOT be deducted. Each started hour MUST be charged at the vehicle's hourly rate.

 - **FR-011**: The total fee MUST equal the parking fee plus the lost-ticket penalty.
 - **FR-012**: On success, the command MUST exit with status 0 and write exactly one line to standard output: a compact JSON object followed by one newline.  The application MUST separate input parsing and validation, tariff definition, fee
 calculation, and command-line handling. The fee calculation MUST be a pure function
 with no input/output operations. The command-line layer MUST remain thin.
 
 ### II. Data-Driven Tariff
 The grace period, hourly rates, daily cap, and any penalties MUST be defined as data
 in one tariff module, separate from the fee calculation function. This keeps tariff
 policy distinct from calculation logic.
 
 ### III. Integer Money and Durations
 Money MUST be represented as whole rupees using integers. Durations MUST be
 represented as whole seconds or minutes using integers. Floats MUST NOT be used for
 money or durations, including during parsing.
 
 ### IV. Deterministic Behavior
 The same input file MUST produce byte-identical output. The program MUST NOT use
 randomness, read the system clock, or make network calls. The feature specification
 MUST state every ordering and rounding rule, including output serialization rules;
 the implementation MUST follow those rules.
 
 ### V. Explicit Input and CLI Contract
 The command line MUST accept exactly one input file path argument and emit a JSON
 result on stdout on success, with exit code 0. Invalid input MUST produce exit code 2
 and a single-line error message on stderr. Expected errors MUST NOT produce stack
 traces. Input validation and error handling MUST be explicit, and invalid input MUST
 never produce partial results.
 
 ## Runtime and Security Constraints
 
 The tool MUST use Python 3.12 or later and only the Python standard library at
 runtime. Development tools including pytest, pytest-cov, ruff, and bandit are
 permitted. The program MUST read only the input file supplied to it.
 
 Secrets MUST NOT be exposed in source code. Credentials, API keys, and `.env` files
 MUST NOT be committed. The program MUST NOT use `eval`, `exec`, `pickle`, or shell
 execution.
 
 ## Quality and Implementation Boundaries
 
 An independent harness MUST enforce all of these quality gates: ruff reports zero
 errors; bandit reports zero medium- or high-severity findings; all tests pass; line
 coverage of `src/` is at least 90%; and every acceptance criterion in the

 Solutions MUST prefer simplicity and maintainability over unnecessary complexity.

Warning

## Aware and Naive Objects[¶](#aware-and-naive-objects "Link to this heading")

Date and time objects may be categorized as “aware” or “naive” depending on whether or not they include time zone information.

With sufficient knowledge of applicable algorithmic and political time adjustments, such as time zone and daylight saving time information, an **aware** object can locate itself relative to other aware objects. An aware object represents a specific moment in time that is not open to interpretation. [\[1\]](#id4)

A **naive** object does not contain enough information to unambiguously locate itself relative to other date/time objects. Whether a naive object represents Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), local time, or time in some other time zone is purely up to the program, just like it is up to the program whether a particular number represents metres, miles, or mass. Naive objects are easy to understand and to work with, at the cost of ignoring some aspects of reality.

For applications requiring aware objects, [`datetime`](#datetime.datetime "datetime.datetime") and [`time`](#datetime.time "datetime.time") objects have an optional time zone information attribute, `tzinfo`, that can be set to an instance of a subclass of the abstract [`tzinfo`](#datetime.tzinfo "datetime.tzinfo") class. These [`tzinfo`](#datetime.tzinfo "datetime.tzinfo") objects capture information about the offset from UTC time, the time zone name, and whether daylight saving time is in effect.

Only one concrete [`tzinfo`](#datetime.tzinfo "datetime.tzinfo") class, the [`timezone`](#datetime.timezone "datetime.timezone") class, is supplied by the `datetime` module. The `timezone` class can represent simple time zones with fixed offsets from UTC, such as UTC itself or North American EST and EDT time zones. Supporting time zones at deeper levels of detail is up to the application. The rules for time adjustment across the world are more political than rational, change frequently, and there is no standard suitable for every application aside from UTC.

sys.addaudithook(_hook_)[¶](#sys.addaudithook "Link to this definition")

Append the callable _hook_ to the list of active auditing hooks for the current (sub)interpreter.

When an auditing event is raised through the [`sys.audit()`](#sys.audit "sys.audit") function, each hook will be called in the order it was added with the event name and the tuple of arguments. Native hooks added by [`PySys_AddAuditHook()`](../c-api/sys.html#c.PySys_AddAuditHook "PySys_AddAuditHook") are called first, followed by hooks added in the current (sub)interpreter. Hooks can then log the event, raise an exception to abort the operation, or terminate the process entirely.

Note that audit hooks are primarily for collecting information about internal or otherwise unobservable actions, whether by Python or libraries written in Python. They are not suitable for implementing a “sandbox”. In particular, malicious code can trivially disable or bypass hooks added using this function. At a minimum, any security-sensitive hooks must be added using the C API [`PySys_AddAuditHook()`](../c-api/sys.html#c.PySys_AddAuditHook "PySys_AddAuditHook") before initialising the runtime, and any modules allowing arbitrary memory modification (such as [`ctypes`](ctypes.html#module-ctypes "ctypes: A foreign function library for Python.")) should be completely removed or closely monitored.

Calling [`sys.addaudithook()`](#sys.addaudithook "sys.addaudithook") will itself raise an auditing event named `sys.addaudithook` with no arguments. If any existing hooks raise an exception derived from [`RuntimeError`](exceptions.html#RuntimeError "RuntimeError"), the new hook will not be added and the exception suppressed. As a result, callers cannot assume that their hook has been added unless they control all existing hooks.

See the [audit events table](audit_events.html#audit-events) for all events raised by CPython, and [**PEP 578**](https://peps.python.org/pep-0578/) for the original design discussion.

# `io` — Core tools for working with streams[¶](#module-io "Link to this heading")

**Source code:** [Lib/io.py](https://github.com/python/cpython/tree/3.12/Lib/io.py)

* * *

## Overview[¶](#overview "Link to this heading")

The [`io`](#module-io "io: Core tools for working with streams.") module provides Python’s main facilities for dealing with various types of I/O. There are three main types of I/O: _text I/O_, _binary I/O_ and _raw I/O_. These are generic categories, and various backing stores can be used for each of them. A concrete object belonging to any of these categories is called a [file object](../glossary.html#term-file-object). Other common terms are _stream_ and _file-like object_.

Independent of its category, each concrete stream object will also have various capabilities: it can be read-only, write-only, or read-write. It can also allow arbitrary random access (seeking forwards or backwards to any location), or only sequential access (for example in the case of a socket or pipe).

All streams are careful about the type of data you give to them. For example giving a [`str`](stdtypes.html#str "str") object to the `write()` method of a binary stream will raise a [`TypeError`](exceptions.html#TypeError "TypeError"). So will giving a [`bytes`](stdtypes.html#bytes "bytes") object to the `write()` method of a text stream.

Changed in version 3.3: Operations that used to raise [`IOError`](exceptions.html#IOError "IOError") now raise [`OSError`](exceptions.html#OSError "OSError"), since [`IOError`](exceptions.html#IOError "IOError") is now an alias of [`OSError`](exceptions.html#OSError "OSError").

### Text I/O[¶](#text-i-o "Link to this heading")

Text I/O expects and produces [`str`](stdtypes.html#str "str") objects. This means that whenever the backing store is natively made of bytes (such as in the case of a file), encoding and decoding of data is made transparently as well as optional translation of platform-specific newline characters.

The easiest way to create a text stream is with [`open()`](functions.html#open "open"), optionally specifying an encoding:

f = open("myfile.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8")

In-memory text streams are also available as [`StringIO`](#io.StringIO "io.StringIO") objects:

f = io.StringIO("some initial text data")

The text stream API is described in detail in the documentation of [`TextIOBase`](#io.TextIOBase "io.TextIOBase").

### Binary I/O[¶](#binary-i-o "Link to this heading")

Binary I/O (also called _buffered I/O_) expects [bytes-like objects](../glossary.html#term-bytes-like-object) and produces [`bytes`](stdtypes.html#bytes "bytes") objects. No encoding, decoding, or newline translation is performed. This category of streams can be used for all kinds of non-text data, and also when manual control over the handling of text data is desired.

The easiest way to create a binary stream is with [`open()`](functions.html#open "open") with `'b'` in the mode string:

f = open("myfile.jpg", "rb")

In-memory binary streams are also available as [`BytesIO`](#io.BytesIO "io.BytesIO") objects:

f = io.BytesIO(b"some initial binary data: \x00\x01")

The binary stream API is described in detail in the docs of [`BufferedIOBase`](#io.BufferedIOBase "io.BufferedIOBase").

Other library modules may provide additional ways to create text or binary streams. See [`socket.socket.makefile()`](socket.html#socket.socket.makefile "socket.socket.makefile") for example.

### Raw I/O[¶](#raw-i-o "Link to this heading")

Raw I/O (also called _unbuffered I/O_) is generally used as a low-level building-block for binary and text streams; it is rarely useful to directly manipulate a raw stream from user code. Nevertheless, you can create a raw stream by opening a file in binary mode with buffering disabled:

f = open("myfile.jpg", "rb", buffering=0)

The raw stream API is described in detail in the docs of [`RawIOBase`](#io.RawIOBase "io.RawIOBase").

## Text Encoding[¶](#text-encoding "Link to this heading")

The default encoding of [`TextIOWrapper`](#io.TextIOWrapper "io.TextIOWrapper") and [`open()`](functions.html#open "open") is locale-specific ([`locale.getencoding()`](locale.html#locale.getencoding "locale.getencoding")).

However, many developers forget to specify the encoding when opening text files encoded in UTF-8 (e.g. JSON, TOML, Markdown, etc…) since most Unix platforms use UTF-8 locale by default. This causes bugs because the locale encoding is not UTF-8 for most Windows users. For example:

# May not work on Windows when non-ASCII characters in the file.
with open("README.md") as f:
    long_description = f.read()

Accordingly, it is highly recommended that you specify the encoding explicitly when opening text files. If you want to use UTF-8, pass `encoding="utf-8"`. To use the current locale encoding, `encoding="locale"` is supported since Python 3.10.

# `argparse` — Parser for command-line options, arguments and subcommands[¶](#module-argparse "Link to this heading")

Added in version 3.2.

**Source code:** [Lib/argparse.py](https://github.com/python/cpython/tree/3.12/Lib/argparse.py)

* * *

The `argparse` module makes it easy to write user-friendly command-line interfaces. The program defines what arguments it requires, and `argparse` will figure out how to parse those out of [`sys.argv`](sys.html#sys.argv "sys.argv"). The `argparse` module also automatically generates help and usage messages. The module will also issue errors when users give the program invalid arguments.

The `argparse` module’s support for command-line interfaces is built around an instance of [`argparse.ArgumentParser`](#argparse.ArgumentParser "argparse.ArgumentParser"). It is a container for argument specifications and has options that apply to the parser as whole:

parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(
                    prog='ProgramName',
                    description='What the program does',
                    epilog='Text at the bottom of help')

The [`ArgumentParser.add_argument()`](#argparse.ArgumentParser.add_argument "argparse.ArgumentParser.add_argument") method attaches individual argument specifications to the parser. It supports positional arguments, options that accept values, and on/off flags:

parser.add_argument('filename')           # positional argument
parser.add_argument('-c', '--count')      # option that takes a value
parser.add_argument('-v', '--verbose',
                    action='store_true')  # on/off flag

The [`ArgumentParser.parse_args()`](#argparse.ArgumentParser.parse_args "argparse.ArgumentParser.parse_args") method runs the parser and places the extracted data in a [`argparse.Namespace`](#argparse.Namespace "argparse.Namespace") object:

args = parser.parse_args()
print(args.filename, args.count, args.verbose)

### prog[¶](#prog "Link to this heading")

By default, [`ArgumentParser`](#argparse.ArgumentParser "argparse.ArgumentParser") calculates the name of the program to display in help messages depending on the way the Python interpreter was run:

*   The Python interpreter name followed by `sys.argv[0]` if a directory or a zipfile was passed as argument.

*   The Python interpreter name followed by `-m` followed by the module or package name if the [`-m`](../using/cmdline.html#cmdoption-m) option was used.

This default is almost always desirable because it will make the help messages match the string that was used to invoke the program on the command line. >>> parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog='myprogram')

>>> parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog='myprogram')
>>> parser.add_argument('--foo', help='foo of the %(prog)s program')

## Aware and Naive Objects[¶](#aware-and-naive-objects "Link to this heading")

Date and time objects may be categorized as “aware” or “naive” depending on whether or not they include time zone information.

With sufficient knowledge of applicable algorithmic and political time adjustments, such as time zone and daylight saving time information, an **aware** object can locate itself relative to other aware objects. An aware object represents a specific moment in time that is not open to interpretation. [\[1\]](#id4)

A **naive** object does not contain enough information to unambiguously locate itself relative to other date/time objects. Whether a naive object represents Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), local time, or time in some other time zone is purely up to the program, just like it is up to the program whether a particular number represents metres, miles, or mass. Naive objects are easy to understand and to work with, at the cost of ignoring some aspects of reality.

For applications requiring aware objects, [`datetime`](#datetime.datetime "datetime.datetime") and [`time`](#datetime.time "datetime.time") objects have an optional time zone information attribute, `tzinfo`, that can be set to an instance of a subclass of the abstract [`tzinfo`](#datetime.tzinfo "datetime.tzinfo") class. These [`tzinfo`](#datetime.tzinfo "datetime.tzinfo") objects capture information about the offset from UTC time, the time zone name, and whether daylight saving time is in effect.

Only one concrete [`tzinfo`](#datetime.tzinfo "datetime.tzinfo") class, the [`timezone`](#datetime.timezone "datetime.timezone") class, is supplied by the `datetime` module. Supporting time zones at deeper levels of detail is up to the application. The rules for time adjustment across the world are more political than rational, change frequently, and there is no standard suitable for every application aside from UTC.

When an auditing event is raised through the [`sys.audit()`](#sys.audit "sys.audit") function, each hook will be called in the order it was added with the event name and the tuple of arguments. Native hooks added by [`PySys_AddAuditHook()`](../c-api/sys.html#c.PySys_AddAuditHook "PySys_AddAuditHook") are called first, followed by hooks added in the current (sub)interpreter. Hooks can then log the event, raise an exception to abort the operation, or terminate the process entirely.

Note that audit hooks are primarily for collecting information about internal or otherwise unobservable actions, whether by Python or libraries written in Python. They are not suitable for implementing a “sandbox”. In particular, malicious code can trivially disable or bypass hooks added using this function. At a minimum, any security-sensitive hooks must be added using the C API [`PySys_AddAuditHook()`](../c-api/sys.html#c.PySys_AddAuditHook "PySys_AddAuditHook") before initialising the runtime, and any modules allowing arbitrary memory modification (such as [`ctypes`](ctypes.html#module-ctypes "ctypes: A foreign function library for Python.")) should be completely removed or closely monitored.

If any existing hooks raise an exception derived from [`RuntimeError`](exceptions.html#RuntimeError "RuntimeError"), the new hook will not be added and the exception suppressed. See the [audit events table](audit_events.html#audit-events) for all events raised by CPython, and [**PEP 578**](https://peps.python.org/pep-0578/) for the original design discussion.

## Overview[¶](#overview "Link to this heading")

The [`io`](#module-io "io: Core tools for working with streams.") module provides Python’s main facilities for dealing with various types of I/O. There are three main types of I/O: _text I/O_, _binary I/O_ and _raw I/O_. These are generic categories, and various backing stores can be used for each of them. A concrete object belonging to any of these categories is called a [file object](../glossary.html#term-file-object). Other common terms are _stream_ and _file-like object_.

Independent of its category, each concrete stream object will also have various capabilities: it can be read-only, write-only, or read-write. It can also allow arbitrary random access (seeking forwards or backwards to any location), or only sequential access (for example in the case of a socket or pipe).

All streams are careful about the type of data you give to them. For example giving a [`str`](stdtypes.html#str "str") object to the `write()` method of a binary stream will raise a [`TypeError`](exceptions.html#TypeError "TypeError"). So will giving a [`bytes`](stdtypes.html#bytes "bytes") object to the `write()` method of a text stream.

Changed in version 3.3: Operations that used to raise [`IOError`](exceptions.html#IOError "IOError") now raise [`OSError`](exceptions.html#OSError "OSError"), since [`IOError`](exceptions.html#IOError "IOError") is now an alias of [`OSError`](exceptions.html#OSError "OSError").

### Text I/O[¶](#text-i-o "Link to this heading")

Text I/O expects and produces [`str`](stdtypes.html#str "str") objects. This means that whenever the backing store is natively made of bytes (such as in the case of a file), encoding and decoding of data is made transparently as well as optional translation of platform-specific newline characters.

The easiest way to create a text stream is with [`open()`](functions.html#open "open"), optionally specifying an encoding:

f = open("myfile.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8")

In-memory text streams are also available as [`StringIO`](#io.StringIO "io.StringIO") objects:

f = io.StringIO("some initial text data")

The text stream API is described in detail in the documentation of [`TextIOBase`](#io.TextIOBase "io.TextIOBase").

### Binary I/O[¶](#binary-i-o "Link to this heading")

Binary I/O (also called _buffered I/O_) expects [bytes-like objects](../glossary.html#term-bytes-like-object) and produces [`bytes`](stdtypes.html#bytes "bytes") objects. No encoding, decoding, or newline translation is performed. This category of streams can be used for all kinds of non-text data, and also when manual control over the handling of text data is desired.

The easiest way to create a binary stream is with [`open()`](functions.html#open "open") with `'b'` in the mode string:

f = open("myfile.jpg", "rb")

In-memory binary streams are also available as [`BytesIO`](#io.BytesIO "io.BytesIO") objects:

f = io.BytesIO(b"some initial binary data: \x00\x01")

The binary stream API is described in detail in the docs of [`BufferedIOBase`](#io.BufferedIOBase "io.BufferedIOBase").

Other library modules may provide additional ways to create text or binary streams. See [`socket.socket.makefile()`](socket.html#socket.socket.makefile "socket.socket.makefile") for example.

### Raw I/O[¶](#raw-i-o "Link to this heading")

Raw I/O (also called _unbuffered I/O_) is generally used as a low-level building-block for binary and text streams; it is rarely useful to directly manipulate a raw stream from user code. Nevertheless, you can create a raw stream by opening a file in binary mode with buffering disabled:

f = open("myfile.jpg", "rb", buffering=0)

The raw stream API is described in detail in the docs of [`RawIOBase`](#io.RawIOBase "io.RawIOBase").

## Text Encoding[¶](#text-encoding "Link to this heading")

The default encoding of [`TextIOWrapper`](#io.TextIOWrapper "io.TextIOWrapper") and [`open()`](functions.html#open "open") is locale-specific ([`locale.getencoding()`](locale.html#locale.getencoding "locale.getencoding")).

However, many developers forget to specify the encoding when opening text files encoded in UTF-8 (e.g. JSON, TOML, Markdown, etc…) since most Unix platforms use UTF-8 locale by default. This causes bugs because the locale encoding is not UTF-8 for most Windows users. For example:

# May not work on Windows when non-ASCII characters in the file.
with open("README.md") as f:
    long_description = f.read()

Accordingly, it is highly recommended that you specify the encoding explicitly when opening text files. If you want to use UTF-8, pass `encoding="utf-8"`. To use the current locale encoding, `encoding="locale"` is supported since Python 3.10.

### Opt-in EncodingWarning[¶](#opt-in-encodingwarning "Link to this heading")

Added in version 3.10: See [**PEP 597**](https://peps.python.org/pep-0597/) for more details.

To find where the default locale encoding is used, you can enable the [`-X warn_default_encoding`](../using/cmdline.html#cmdoption-X) command line option or set the [`PYTHONWARNDEFAULTENCODING`](../using/cmdline.html#envvar-PYTHONWARNDEFAULTENCODING) environment variable, which will emit an [`EncodingWarning`](exceptions.html#EncodingWarning "EncodingWarning") when the default encoding is used.

If you are providing an API that uses [`open()`](functions.html#open "open") or [`TextIOWrapper`](#io.TextIOWrapper "io.TextIOWrapper") and passes `encoding=None` as a parameter, you can use [`text_encoding()`](#io.text_encoding "io.text_encoding") so that callers of the API will emit an [`EncodingWarning`](exceptions.html#EncodingWarning "EncodingWarning") if they don’t pass an `encoding`. However, please consider using UTF-8 by default (i.e. `encoding="utf-8"`) for new APIs.

# `decimal` — Decimal fixed-point and floating-point arithmetic[¶](#module-decimal "Link to this heading")

**Source code:** [Lib/decimal.py](https://github.com/python/cpython/tree/3.12/Lib/decimal.py)

* * *

The [`decimal`](#module-decimal "decimal: Implementation of the General Decimal Arithmetic  Specification.") module provides support for fast correctly rounded decimal floating-point arithmetic. It offers several advantages over the [`float`](functions.html#float "float") datatype:

*   Decimal “is based on a floating-point model which was designed with people in mind, and necessarily has a paramount guiding principle – computers must provide an arithmetic that works in the same way as the arithmetic that people learn at school.” – excerpt from the decimal arithmetic specification.

*   Decimal numbers can be represented exactly. In contrast, numbers like `1.1` and `2.2` do not have exact representations in binary floating point. End users typically would not expect `1.1 + 2.2` to display as `3.3000000000000003` as it does with binary floating point.

*   The exactness carries over into arithmetic. In decimal floating point, `0.1
    + 0.1 + 0.1 - 0.3` is exactly equal to zero. In binary floating point, the result is `5.5511151231257827e-017`. While near to zero, the differences prevent reliable equality testing and differences can accumulate. For this reason, decimal is preferred in accounting applications which have strict equality invariants.

*   The decimal module incorporates a notion of significant places so that `1.30
    + 1.20` is `2.50`. The trailing zero is kept to indicate significance. This is the customary presentation for monetary applications. For multiplication, the “schoolbook” approach uses all the figures in the multiplicands. For instance, `1.3 * 1.2` gives `1.56` while `1.30 *
    1.20` gives `1.5600`.

*   Unlike hardware based binary floating point, the decimal module has a user alterable precision (defaulting to 28 places) which can be as large as needed for a given problem:

    >>> from decimal import *
    >>> getcontext().prec = 6
    >>> Decimal(1) / Decimal(7)
    Decimal('0.142857')
    >>> getcontext().prec = 28
    >>> Decimal(1) / Decimal(7)
    Decimal('0.1428571428571428571428571429')

*   Both binary and decimal floating point are implemented in terms of published standards. While the built-in float type exposes only a modest portion of its capabilities, the decimal module exposes all required parts of the standard. When needed, the programmer has full control over rounding and signal handling. This includes an option to enforce exact arithmetic by using exceptions to block any inexact operations.

*   The decimal module was designed to support “without prejudice, both exact unrounded decimal arithmetic (sometimes called fixed-point arithmetic) and rounded floating-point arithmetic.” – excerpt from the decimal arithmetic specification.

The module design is centered around three concepts: the decimal number, the context for arithmetic, and signals.

A decimal number is immutable. It has a sign, coefficient digits, and an exponent. To preserve significance, the coefficient digits do not truncate trailing zeros. Decimals also include special values such as `Infinity`, `-Infinity`, and `NaN`. The standard also differentiates `-0` from `+0`.

The context for arithmetic is an environment specifying precision, rounding rules, limits on exponents, flags indicating the results of operations, and trap enablers which determine whether signals are treated as exceptions. Supports the following objects and types by default:

| Python                                 | JSON   |
| -------------------------------------- | ------ |
| dict                                   | object |
| list, tuple                            | array  |

If _ensure\_ascii_ is true (the default), the output is guaranteed to have all incoming non-ASCII characters escaped. If _ensure\_ascii_ is false, these characters will be output as-is.

If _check\_circular_ is true (the default), then lists, dicts, and custom encoded objects will be checked for circular references during encoding to prevent an infinite recursion (which would cause a [`RecursionError`](exceptions.html#RecursionError "RecursionError")). If _allow\_nan_ is true (the default), then `NaN`, `Infinity`, and `-Infinity` will be encoded as such. Otherwise, it will be a [`ValueError`](exceptions.html#ValueError "ValueError") to encode such floats.
